title: The destination, and the grades ladder
paras: Chartered Town Planner means chartered membership of the Institute — the letters M-R-T-P-I after your name, the mark many senior and consultancy roles expect or require. You get there by passing the Assessment of Professional Competence; the routes are just different ways of reaching that same assessment. Exact fees, word counts and links are in the written guide.

Picture the grades as a ladder. Student while on an accredited course, usually free. Licentiate once you hold an accredited qualification and are working towards the assessment. Associate, a professional grade for those contributing to planning without a fully accredited qualification, and a stepping stone to chartered. Chartered, the goal, reached by passing the assessment. And Fellow, a senior grade for experienced chartered members, awarded on nomination.

title: The two things every route needs
paras: Chartered status comes down to two things: an accredited academic grounding, and proven professional competence through experience, tested by the assessment. The routes differ mainly in the academic side. Accreditation covers two parts — a spatial planning component, the broad knowledge every planner needs, and a specialist component, deeper expertise in a chosen area. A fully accredited qualification, often a combined Masters, covers both; some undergraduate degrees cover only spatial planning, so you top up with an accredited specialist Masters.

So the rule is: check any course is actually accredited, and whether it's combined or only partial, because that tells you if you need anything further. And academic knowledge alone doesn't make you chartered — you show, through the assessment, that you can apply planning skills competently in practice, from real experience under experienced guidance.

title: Routes at a glance
paras: Routes at a glance — find your starting point, then read the section that follows. Timings are indicative, so confirm the current requirements.

Accredited planning Masters or combined degree: join as a Licentiate, two years' experience with one as a Licentiate, pass the assessment — two to three years. Accredited undergraduate in spatial planning only: top up with a specialist Masters first, an extra one to two years. Degree in another subject: an accredited conversion Masters plus the assessment, or the apprenticeship — one to two years studying, then two to three.

Working in planning with no accredited degree: the Associate assessment, study, or the apprenticeship — become an Associate on your experience, then progress to Chartered, around four to five years. To earn while you learn: the Level 7 apprenticeship — your employer sponsors you, you combine work and university, finishing with an accredited Masters and end-point assessment in three to four years. Surveyor or other built-environment professional: the Experienced Practitioner assessment, or a Masters plus the standard one, timing tracking experience.

title: If you have an accredited planning degree
paras: The most direct route. Hold a fully accredited planning qualification — an accredited Masters, or an undergraduate degree covering both spatial planning and specialist parts — and you join as a Licentiate and start towards the assessment. You'll need at least two years' professional planning experience — full-time equivalent, part-time pro-rata — with at least one year as a registered Licentiate, then you submit. Most accredited graduates are chartered two to three years after finishing, alongside a normal job.

If your undergraduate degree is only partly accredited, covering just spatial planning, you're part way there: top up with an accredited specialist Masters, often one year full-time or two part-time, for the full grounding and access to the assessment. Check what your degree was accredited for first.

title: If your degree is in another subject
paras: Many planners did their first degree in something else — geography, law, architecture, economics, history — and converted. The cleanest route is an accredited conversion Masters, built for graduates of any discipline and assuming no prior study — typically one year full-time or two part-time, with distance versions so you can study while you work. Finish an accredited combined Masters and you're where any accredited graduate is: join as a Licentiate and take the assessment.

If studying first doesn't suit, there are alternatives. Employed in a planning role, the apprenticeship gets you the Masters and chartered status while working, without tuition fees; already building experience, the Associate and Experienced Practitioner routes may fit. But for most non-planning graduates free to study, an accredited Masters is the direct answer.

title: If you work in planning without an accredited degree
paras: Plenty of capable people work in planning — support officers, technicians, enforcement or validation staff, administrators — without an accredited qualification and want to become chartered. Three realistic options.

The first is the Associate route, for those contributing to planning without a fully accredited qualification. Depending on your background you'll need roughly two to seven years of relevant experience to apply, and success gives you the grade of Associate — recognised in its own right, and a stepping stone, with a defined route on to full Chartered. Allow four to five years to chartered this way.

The second is to study for an accredited qualification part-time or by distance learning while keeping your job, then take the assessment. The third is the apprenticeship: if your employer backs it, the Level 7 route lets you earn while you learn, gain the Masters and chartered status together, with the training funded.

title: If you are a surveyor or other built-environment professional
paras: Surveyors, architects, engineers and lawyers often move into planning. But the Institute doesn't automatically recognise another body's membership — whichever door you came through, to become chartered here you satisfy its requirements and competencies. The route most relevant to an established professional is the Experienced Practitioner one, for substantial planning experience — broadly five to ten years, depending on qualifications — who can demonstrate the competencies at a higher level. It expressly caters for related built-environment professionals and those qualified overseas, and it's more demanding than the standard assessment, but it doesn't send you back to university if your experience is strong enough.
If your experience isn't deep enough yet, the ordinary answer applies — an accredited, often part-time, Masters and the standard assessment, or the apprenticeship if you're employed.

title: The degree apprenticeship route
paras: The Level 7 degree apprenticeship has become one of the most important routes in. Employed in a planning role, your employer sponsors you. You typically work four days a week and study one, over roughly three to four years depending on prior qualifications, completing an accredited Masters along the way. At the end you sit an end-point assessment — a professional discussion and a submission equivalent to the ordinary one — coming out with both the accredited Masters and chartered membership.

The attraction is financial: training's funded through the apprenticeship levy and the employer, so you don't pay tuition fees. The catch is you need an employer willing to sponsor you and give you study time, and you must meet the entry requirements. If you're in a planning team, ask — many authorities and consultancies run apprentices.

title: The APC in detail
paras: Whatever your route, all roads end at the Assessment of Professional Competence — proving you can practise as a chartered planner. The standard is the Licentiate version; the Associate, Experienced Practitioner and apprenticeship ones follow the same idea, differing in level and format. It's a written submission of around five and a half thousand words, give or take ten per cent, in three parts: a practical experience statement, about a thousand words, on the range of your experience; a professional competence statement, about three thousand words — the core — using one to three case studies from your own work to demonstrate all ten competencies; and a professional development plan, about fifteen hundred words, looking forward a couple of years. Confirm the current word counts and competency list before you write.

Alongside the statements you provide a reflective journal covering at least a year of full-time-equivalent experience, corroborator declarations from colleagues, a sponsor declaration from a Chartered Town Planner, and your degree certificates. A mentor isn't always compulsory but it's strongly advised.

Trained assessors mark it against the competencies, each at the required level. Fall short and you're referred with feedback, and can resubmit within two years of your first attempt without starting over; after that, a fresh application. The competencies reward applied judgement, not recited knowledge — so pick case studies where you made or shaped decisions and write what you did and why.

title: Time, money and CPD
paras: Time first. From an accredited Masters, expect two to three years of practice before chartered; from a standing start in another discipline, add one to two years of study on the front. The apprenticeship is around three to four years all in, and the Associate and Experienced Practitioner routes track your experience. There's no minimum age and no maximum time limit. On money: subscription fees vary by grade — student usually free, Licentiate and Chartered charged annually — plus an assessment fee for the submission. Accredited Masters carry tuition fees unless you take the apprenticeship, which is funded. The figures change yearly, so check the current ones.
And once chartered, it isn't the finish line: members must do continuing professional development each year, keep a record, and abide by the Code of Professional Conduct.

title: Practical tips
paras: Check accreditation before you enrol, and whether it's combined or partial. Start your reflective journal on day one, not the month before you submit. Get a mentor early, ideally a Chartered Town Planner who'll also sponsor you.
And don't neglect the development plan section; it's assessed, not a formality, and a thin one costs marks.

If you're employed, ask about the apprenticeship — funded training, a salary, and chartered status at the end. And use your local network: branches, Young Planners groups and assessment workshops are free. The routes, competencies, word counts, experience requirements and fees get reviewed periodically, so confirm the current detail before you commit — this guide explains the routes, it isn't a substitute for the Institute's own candidate guidance.
